title: Payment fraud and business email compromise
summary: For anyone who pays, approves or changes vendor details. How invoice fraud and CEO fraud work, and the verification steps that stop them.
body_md:
## The most expensive email scam

Business email compromise (BEC) costs companies more than ransomware. Criminals impersonate, or actually take over
the email of, a vendor, an executive or a colleague, then redirect a real payment to their own account. Losses are
rarely recovered.

## Common versions

- **Changed bank details.** A "vendor" writes that their bank account has changed and asks you to pay this month's
  invoice to the new account. Often the email comes from the vendor's real, hacked mailbox, in an existing thread.
- **CEO or CFO fraud.** An urgent, confidential request from a leader to make a payment, buy gift cards or send
  employee tax data, often timed when they're travelling.
- **Fake invoices** for services you never ordered, or duplicates of real invoices.
- **Payroll diversion.** An "employee" asks HR to change the account their salary goes to.

## Controls that stop it

1. **Call back to verify any bank-detail change**, using a phone number from your vendor master file or the
   original contract, never one in the email. Record who you spoke to.
2. **Two people for payments**: one creates, another approves, especially for new payees and changed details.
3. **Hold period**: payments to newly changed accounts wait a set time while verification completes.
4. **No exceptions for urgency or seniority.** A real leader will understand a verification call.
5. **Check the email address**, not just the display name; look for look-alike domains (`acrne.in` vs `acme.in`).
6. **Watch for reply-to tricks**: the reply goes to a different address than the sender.

## If something seems wrong

Stop the payment if possible, call the bank immediately to try to recall the transfer, report on **1930** or
cybercrime.gov.in, and tell the security team. Speed is the only thing that recovers money.

scenarios.subject: RE: Invoice 4471 - updated remittance details
scenarios.body: Hi, as discussed our banking partner has changed. Please process invoice 4471 to the new account below from this cycle. Our old account is under audit so payments there will bounce.
scenarios.explain: Even in a real thread, a bank change needs a call-back on a known number. Hacked mailboxes reply inside genuine threads.

scenarios.subject: PO-2291 approved
scenarios.body: Purchase order PO-2291 for Rs 48,000 was approved by Meera S. View it in the procurement system.
scenarios.explain: A system notification from your own domain about an expected workflow, pointing you to the system itself.

quiz.q: A long-time supplier emails, in an existing thread, asking you to pay this month's invoice to a new bank account. What do you do?
options: Update the details; the thread is genuine
Call the supplier on the number in your vendor file to verify before changing anything
Reply to the email to confirm

quiz.q: The CEO emails asking for an urgent, confidential transfer while travelling. What's right?
options: Make the transfer; it's the CEO
Verify through a separate channel and follow the normal approval process
Reply asking if it's really them

quiz.q: Why do payments need two people?
options: One person can't create and approve a fraudulent or mistaken payment alone

quiz.q: Which sender address is suspicious for a supplier called Acme India (acme.in)?
You realise a payment went to a fraudulent account an hour ago. What first?
options: Wait for the vendor to complain
Call the bank to recall it, report on 1930, and tell security
